title: Event Triggered Execution: Screensaver
summary: A Windows screensaver is an executable with the .scr extension that the desktop starts after a configured period of user inactivity, and the settings that control it live in the registry under the current user's Control Panel desktop key. Four values decide the behaviour: the one that names the screensaver program, the one that enables the feature, the one that decides whether a password is required to return to the desktop, and the one that sets the inactivity timeout. Because the screensaver is simply a program, an attacker who can write those values can name a payload instead of a real screensaver and have it execute on a timer that users understand and rarely question. The accompanying changes are just as telling as the payload itself. Lowering the timeout, forcing the feature on, and switching off the password requirement all make the trigger fire sooner or make the session easier to resume without a password, and the last of those has its own value for an attacker who returns to the machine physically or over a remote session. Detractors matter here: the same values are legitimately set by group policy, by the user, and by software such as remote support tools. Detection compares the configured program path with approved screensaver locations and signatures and correlates it with process creation events in which the screensaver program spawns children it should not.

beginner.definition: A screensaver is a program that starts when you leave the computer idle for a while, usually to hide the screen. On Windows these programs use the file ending .scr, and the settings for them are stored in the registry. This technique is when an attacker points that setting at their own program.
beginner.whyItMatters: The attacker's program then runs by itself whenever the machine sits idle. Idle time happens every day, so the code runs again and again without any user action. Some attackers also disable the setting that asks for a password, which helps them return to the session later. It is easy to miss because screensavers are boring and familiar.
howItWorks: The attacker places their program on the disk and gives it the .scr file ending, or names a real one.
They edit a registry value that records which screensaver program Windows should run.
They set the value that switches the screensaver feature on, so it will actually start.
They set a timeout value, often a short one, so idle time triggers the program quickly.
They may set the password value so that unlocking is not required when the session resumes.
When the machine stays idle for the chosen time, Windows starts the program as the logged-in user.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital night desk that hands out a sleeping pill to any patient who has been quiet for an hour. A stranger edits the ward sheet so that the hourly dose is now a different medicine kept in their own cupboard. Nobody questions a routine dose, and it is given again every quiet hour. The staff believe they are following the usual schedule.
takeaways: A .scr file is just a program, so it can contain anything a normal executable can.
Check the configured screensaver path, its signature, and where the file lives.
A screensaver setting that removes the unlock password is a warning sign on its own.

objectives: Explain how Windows decides when to start a screensaver.
Name the registry values that control screensaver behaviour and location.
Explain why a .scr file can carry any executable content.
Explain how a weakened unlock setting adds risk for the user session.
Describe the process creation evidence left when a screensaver runs.
